title: Giving reasons: as, because, etc.; for and with
subtitle: as / since / seeing that; due to; with
summary: Give reasons with as, because, since and seeing that, choose between because of, due to and owing to, and use for and with + a noun phrase.

lesson.heading: as, because, seeing that, seeing as, since
lesson.text: Any of these can begin a clause that gives the reason for a particular situation. It is common and perfectly acceptable for **because** to begin a sentence.

examples.text: **As** it was getting late, I decided I should go home.
We must be near the beach, **because** I can hear the waves.
**Since** he was going to be away on his birthday, we celebrated before he left.
We could go and visit Natalia, **seeing that** we have to drive past her house anyway.
**Because** everything looked different, I had no idea where to go.

lesson.heading: because or so?

left.label: because introduces the reason
examples: **Because** my mother's ill, I won't be able to come.

right.label: so introduces the result
examples: My mother's ill, **so** I won't be able to come.

lesson.note: To give reasons in spoken English we most often use because; so is just as common for expressing the same idea the other way round.

lesson.heading: How formal is each one?
lesson.text: When it means 'because', **since** is rather formal: it is uncommon in conversation but frequent in academic writing. **Seeing that** belongs to informal English, and some people also use **seeing as** in informal speech.

examples.text: I had to go outside **because** I was feeling awful.
examples.note: since is unlikely in such an informal context

examples.text: The results of this analysis can be easily compared to future observations **since** satellite coverage will remain continuous.
examples.note: more likely than because in this formal context

examples.text: Joel just had to apologise, **seeing that / as** he knew he'd made a mistake.

lesson.heading: for, in that, inasmuch as
lesson.text: In formal or literary written English we can also introduce a reason with **for**, **in that** or, less commonly, **inasmuch as**. For is a formal alternative to 'because'; in that and inasmuch as introduce clauses which clarify what has been said by adding detail.

examples.text: We must begin planning now, **for** the future may bring unexpected changes.
examples.wrong: For the future may bring unexpected changes, we must begin planning now

examples.text: The film is unusual **in that** it features only four actors.
examples.note: or In that ..., the film is ...

examples.text: Clara and I have quite an easy life, **inasmuch as** neither of us has to work too hard but we earn quite a lot of money.

lesson.note: An in that or inasmuch as clause can come first; a for-clause cannot.

lesson.heading: because of, due to, owing to + noun phrase
lesson.text: These prepositions go before a noun or noun phrase to give a reason. Note that **because** alone is never used before a noun phrase.

examples.text: We were delayed **because of** an accident.
She was unable to run **owing to / due to** a leg injury.
We have less money to spend **owing to / due to** budget cuts.
We were delayed **because there was** an accident.

lesson.heading: due to or owing to after be?
lesson.text: In current English we usually avoid **owing to** directly after a form of *be*. But owing to is used after be + a degree adverb such as entirely, largely, mainly or partly, and either can be used in the pattern *it was due to / owing to ... that*.

examples.text: The company's success is **due to** the new director.
examples.wrong: is owing to the new director

examples.text: The low election turnout was partly **due to / owing to** the bad weather.
**It was owing to** his encouragement **that** she applied for the job.
examples.note: or It was due to ... that

lesson.heading: for and with + noun phrase
lesson.text: **For** and **with** followed by a noun phrase can also give a reason: for means 'as a result of', and with means 'as a result of there being'.

examples.text: She was looking all the better **for** her stay in hospital.
**With** so many people ill, the meeting was cancelled.
**With** her father in hospital, Olivia went to stay with her aunt.

lesson.text: Test what follows: a clause with its own subject and verb takes *because / as / since*; a noun phrase takes *because of / due to / owing to / for / with*.

exercises.prompt: ___ it was getting late, I decided I should go home.
exercises.explanation: As can begin a reason clause; a for-clause can never come first, and owing to needs a noun phrase.

exercises.prompt: He sent the soup back ___ there was a fly in it.
exercises.explanation: A full clause follows, so because - not because of.

exercises.prompt: Match each statement to the reason that goes with it.

pairs.left: Since the train was delayed for more than an hour,
pairs.right: passengers were given a full refund.

pairs.left: Because I'm trying to lose weight,
As the guest lecturer was late,
pairs.right: Dr Gomez spoke about his research instead.

pairs.left: We were recommended to buy the textbook second-hand since
pairs.right: a new copy would be very expensive.

pairs.left: You should never walk under a ladder because

exercises.prompt: I couldn't speak to Jacob ___ his mobile was switched off.
exercises.explanation: His mobile was switched off is a clause, so it needs because.

exercises.statement: We were delayed because an accident.
exercises.explanation: We were delayed because of an accident. / ... because there was an accident. Because alone cannot go before a noun phrase.

exercises.prompt: The cancellation of the competition is ___ lack of interest.
exercises.explanation: We avoid owing to directly after a form of be.

exercises.prompt: The popularity of the restaurant is largely ___ its central location.
exercises.explanation: After be + a degree adverb such as largely, both are possible.

exercises.statement: The film is unusual in that it features only four actors.
exercises.explanation: Correct. In that introduces a clause that clarifies what has just been said by adding detail.

exercises.prompt: Does each reason word or phrase come before a clause (with its own subject and verb) or before a noun phrase?

exercises.answer: With so many people ill, the meeting was cancelled.
exercises.explanation: With + a noun phrase means 'as a result of there being'.

exercises.prompt: ___ my money running out, I got a job as a street sweeper.
exercises.explanation: With + noun phrase + -ing is a neat way of packing a reason into a phrase.

exercises.prompt: I felt a lot fitter ___ all the exercise I was doing.
exercises.explanation: Both work here: for and with + a noun phrase can mean 'as a result of'.
